title: Crush
full_review:
Each week, three single women share gin, cigarettes and pathetic stories about awful dates or long lonely evenings in the trite drama "Crush" (Sony Pictures Classics). The winner gets a box of gooey chocolates.

Set in a cozy English village where everyone has big, beautiful homes and lush gardens, "Crush" is writer-director John McKay's first effort. His script lays out the narrative all too neatly, which in turn makes for a predictable and flat film. McKay is unable to handle the sharp transition the movie makes in its last third. The movie goes from lighthearted romp to grave drama in a drastic tone change before unsuccessfully trying to right itself to a an all's-well-that-ends-well finale. And the May-December fling that blossoms into to true love is never quite believable, although the script insists it is.

Andie MacDowell stars as Kate, the unlikely headmistress of the local private school who breaks out of the trio's unhealthy cycle of bashing men, for which she is quickly rebuked by her two friends. Molly (Anna Chancellor), a doctor, three times divorced and with a biting sense of humor, is highly suspicious of Kate's newfound happiness with Jed (Kenny Doughty), a 25-year-old hunk who was once Kate's student and is now Kate's lover. Though not as vehement in her disapproval as Molly is, Janine (Imelda Staunton), the town's chief constable, divorced herself with a teen-age son, also withholds her blessing of the couple.

Things heat up when Kate announces Jed and she are to be married. Here the narrative takes a nasty turn. Molly, telling herself she is only saving her friend from being tragically hurt and disappointed, whisks Kate away for a shopping spree in Paris and discloses Jed's past police record. When this fails to break up the couple, Molly tries to seduce Jed and present the evidence of his infidelity (as video taped by Janine) to Kate. But the scheme backfires in a grievous manner and the film cannot recover.

"Crush" is very casual in its attitude about sex. Minutes after meeting Jed, an organist (several unfunny jokes about Jed's "organ" are repeated ad nauseam) for the local crematory, Kate and Jed are coupling in the graveyard, the first of many lovers' trysts. The women take the attitude of sex as sport, without ever speaking of any intimate bond between a man and a woman.

Most of the performances are fair, with the exception of Chancellor, to whom the viewer's attention goes when she's on screen. She allows the audience to penetrate beyond her unsympathetic character's acid tongue to reveal a woman hiding a broken, aching heart who longs to love and be loved. MacDowell cannot go much deeper than the surface with Kate, relying on a costume change to convey a change in her character's emotions.

In the end, the film is supposed to be about forgiveness and the enduring bond of female friendship. But the predictable proceedings are more bitter than sweet as the British romancer borrows from other such films ("Four Weddings and a Funeral" comes to mind) without improving on the material.

Due to several sexual encounters and references, a same-sex kiss and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
